question: Should Arjuna fight the battle in which his elders, teachers and kinsmen stand on the other side?

sides.party: Arjuna's resolve 'I will not fight' (2.9), as Kṛṣṇa restates it at 18.59
arguments: Restated in ch. 18 only as a resolve made from the sense of 'I' (ahaṅkāra), without argument (18.59).

sides.position: Renouncing all actions to Kṛṣṇa in thought, with thought on him, Arjuna should act; his resolve not to fight is vain; he should take refuge in the Lord.
arguments: With thought on Kṛṣṇa he will cross all difficulties by his grace; from the sense of 'I' he would perish (18.57–58).
His nature will compel him; bound by nature-born action he will do even unwillingly what he does not wish (18.59–60).
One whose disposition is not shaped by the sense of 'I' and whose understanding is not stained does not slay though slaying, and is not bound (18.17).
The Lord in the heart moves all beings by his māyā; take refuge in him (18.61–62).
Not fleeing in battle is a kṣatriya's nature-born action (18.43).
Having reflected fully, do as you wish (18.63); relinquishing all dharmas, come to me for refuge (18.66).

historical_debates.name: The dialogue at Kurukṣetra
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Arjuna declares his delusion destroyed and his doubts gone, and says 'I will do your word' (18.73); Sañjaya holds that where Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna are there is victory (18.78).

historical_debates.name: Outcome within the dialogue
historical_debates.accounts: Arjuna answers that his delusion is destroyed, his memory regained, his doubt gone, and that he will do Kṛṣṇa's word (18.73).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Within the text: Arjuna accepts Kṛṣṇa's instruction (18.73).

notes: Contribution of the closing chunk only; the opening sides are in chs. 1–3 (A). Within the text the outcome is Arjuna's 'I will do your word' (18.73); Sañjaya's verdict follows (18.78).

question: Is the renunciation of action or the yoga of action better? (BhG 3.1–8, 5.1–6, 6.1–4, 18.1–12)

sides.party: Some thinkers (eke manīṣiṇaḥ), unnamed in the text (BhG 18.3a)
sides.position: As reported at BhG 18.3a (holders unnamed, 'some thinkers'): action is to be abandoned as faulty.
arguments: Stated as a reported view only; the text gives no argument for it.

sides.position: As reported at BhG 18.3b (holders unnamed, 'others'): acts of sacrifice, giving and austerity are not to be abandoned.
arguments: Stated as a reported view only.

sides.position: Sacrifice, giving and austerity are not to be given up but done, giving up attachment and fruit; relinquishment is threefold; the relinquisher is the one who gives up the fruit of action.
arguments: Sacrifice, giving and austerity purify the wise (18.5).
Renouncing prescribed action is not fitting; doing it from delusion is tāmasic, from fear of hardship rājasic, and only doing it as duty without attachment and fruit is sāttvic (18.7–9).
An embodied being cannot give up actions entirely, so the relinquisher is the one who gives up the fruit (18.11).
The threefold fruit of action comes after death to non-relinquishers, never to renouncers (18.12).

notes: Extractor A records only the sides as ch. 18 states them; the text itself names no holders of the two reported views (commentators' attributions are theirs). Extractor B contribution from BhG 18.1–12: the text itself records the two views of 18.3 and then Kṛṣṇa's decision. Later commentators' identification of the two views (e.g. with Sāṃkhya and Mīmāṃsā) is not in the text.
